newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Britain's foxhunters feel endangered.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Britain's foxhunters feel endangered.

text.p: Britain's foxhunters feel like an endangered species.

At the neatly maintained kennels of the Zetland Hunt in Yorkshire, northern England, foxhound puppies play on the grass as they always have and the local blacksmith is shoeing horses as his father did before him.
But the air of normality masks real anger among hunt staff that their way of life could soon be destroyed by politicians with little understanding of country ways.
With the general election just two days away, many country dwellers fear that if the Labour Party forms the new government, as seems increasingly likely, fox hunting will be banned.

Such a ban would almost certainly force Britain's more than 300 hunts to close, thus ending one of the country's most colourful and traditional sights -- scarlet-coated riders and a pack of hounds in hot pursuit of a speeding fox.
REPERCUSSIONS
Outlawing foxhunting would also mean the loss of up to 33,000 jobs, according to the British Field Sports Society.
Apart from putting hunt staff on the dole, the knock-on effect of a ban would affect thousands more people working as saddlers, feed merchants, vets and in other trades associated with hunting.
"We are an endangered species," said David Jukes, huntsman with the Zetland. "We are under threat from towny politicians making decisions about things they don't know anything about."
Blacksmith Ian Tweddle said nearly threequarters of his business is related to hunting.
"If there was no hunting, I would be taking three or four days a week off," he said.

The possibility of a ban on hunting has also aroused fears among fishermen and those who shoot game that they could be next in line for the attention of the animal rights activists who have clashed, often violently, with foxhunters.
FREE VOTE PROMISED

Labour has promised in its election manifesto to allow a free vote -- in which members are allowed to follow their consciences rather than the party line -- on whether hunting with hounds should be banned by law.

Whether a ban becomes law would depend on the vagaries of Britain's arcane parliamentary system, with opposition expected from the unelected upper House of Lords and members of the lower House of Commons with rural seats.
Labour's spokesman for rural affairs, Elliot Morley, has already said he wants to bring in a ban on land owned by the Ministry of Defence or the state-run Forestry Commission.
The National Trust, a heritage organisation, recently decided to ban stag hunting on its land following a scientific report which found that the practice was cruel.

Members of Parliament opposed to hunting -- mostly Labour but also drawn to a lesser extent from the other main parties -- argue that foxhunting is cruel and should be consigned to history like bear- or badger-baiting.
The hunting lobby says hunting is the best means of controlling foxes and that other methods such as shooting, snaring or gassing are worse.
"It would be a free-for-all, with every lad out with a lamp and a gun," said Jukes. "There is a lot of talk about banning foxhunting but no-one talks about the fox."
He added: "Hunting is well organised. It has taken 300 years to evolve."
What hunting enthusiasts fear as much as anything is the loss of a way of life that has formed an integral part of the British countryside for centuries.
Hunting has long been celebrated in English literature and art and for thousands of people across the country, a day out with the hunt is the high point of their week.
The Zetland hounds are followed by about 80 people on horseback. And following them around the lanes are the same number of cars and even more enthusiasts on foot and on bicycles.

Angie Vaux, one of four joint masters of the Zetland Hunt, rejects any suggestion that hunting is a preserve of the upper classes, listing farmers, a milkman, a plumber, an accountant and cook among the hunt's regular subscribers.
Not only would the social fabric of the countryside suffer if there were a ban on hunting, said Vaux, so would its very appearance.

Hunts take care to preserve hedgerows, which they like to jump their horses over, and coverts, which provide shelter for foxes and other wildlife. An end to hunting could tempt farmers to plough these up in order to increase their crop areas.
One solution put forward by animal rights supporters is that hunts should take up drag-hunting, in which they ride after hounds pursuing an artifical scent rather than a fox.
This is dismissed as unrealistic by the hunting lobby, who say it will never be accepted by farmers who allow the hunt on their land in order to keep foxes down.
For the hunting lobby, a lot will now depend on whether they can mobilise enough political muscle to fight their corner.

Rural workers have formed a new trade union, the Union of Country Sports Workers, and a leading publication, The Field, has urged readers to vote against more than 70 anti-hunting MPs who are defending marginal seats.
Jukes admits that he is worried about the future for his wife and two children. At the very least they stand to lose their house, which is owned by the Zetland Hunt.
"In the old days retired huntsmen used to take on a pub, but there won't be enough pubs to go round," he said.
